leetcode-overview.tldr:
• Nine problems; three patterns solve almost all: semaphore baton passing, shared state + condition wait, barrier per round.
  • Semaphores fit turn-taking because a permit can be released by another thread.
  • Avoid busy waiting: it burns CPU and often times out.
  • Be ready to give a second solution with a different primitive.
leetcode-overview.body:
LeetCode's Concurrency category contains nine problems. Every solution class below uses LeetCode's exact signatures, so you can paste it straight into the editor; each problem also has a small harness to run and verify locally.

# Problem Difficulty Premium Core idea Tools used here
1114 Print in Order Easy no enforce A → B → C CountDownLatch, Semaphore, wait/notify
1115 Print FooBar Alternately Medium no strict turn-taking between 2 threads Semaphore, Lock + Condition, wait/notify
1116 Print Zero Even Odd Medium no 3-way turn-taking with a router Semaphore, wait/notify state machine
1117 Building H2O Medium no group threads 2 + 1 Semaphore + CyclicBarrier, Semaphore only
1195 Fizz Buzz Multithreaded Medium no 4 threads share one counter wait/notify, CyclicBarrier, Semaphore dispatcher
1226 The Dining Philosophers Medium no avoid deadlock on shared forks lock ordering, Semaphore(4), global lock
1188 Design Bounded Blocking Queue Medium yes producer–consumer buffer Lock + 2 Conditions, Semaphores
1242 Web Crawler Multithreaded Medium yes parallel BFS without duplicates ExecutorService, concurrent set, pending counter
1279 Traffic Light Controlled Intersection Easy yes mutual exclusion + state synchronized, ReentrantLock

Three patterns cover almost every ordering problem

  1. Semaphore hand-off (baton passing). One semaphore per "turn". A thread waits on its own semaphore, does its step, then releases the next thread's semaphore. Only the starting semaphore has 1 permit; the rest start at 0. Used in 1114, 1115, 1116.
  2. Shared state + condition wait. Keep a state/turn variable guarded by a lock; each thread waits while (state != mine), acts, updates state, and wakes the others (notifyAll / signalAll). Most general; easy to extend to N threads. Used in every problem as an alternative.
  3. Barrier per round. Every thread iterates over the same rounds and meets at a CyclicBarrier after each one, so they stay in lock-step. Used in 1117 and 1195.

Interview tip whichever primitive you choose, say why: "a semaphore models a turn without ownership, so thread A can release thread B's permit", or "a barrier keeps all four threads on the same number". Interviewers often ask for a second solution with a different primitive.

Anti-pattern: busy waiting. while (turn != 2) { } on a volatile field is correct for visibility but burns a CPU core and can time out on LeetCode. Use blocking primitives; if you must spin, call Thread.onSpinWait() or Thread.yield() inside the loop.

leetcode-printinorder.tldr:
• Two one-shot dependencies: CountDownLatch(1) per step is the most literal model.
  • Semaphores starting at 0 work too and can be reused if the sequence repeats.
  • A shared stage counter with wait/notifyAll generalizes to N steps.
  • Verify by starting threads in every permutation.

leetcode-foobar.tldr:
• Strict alternation between two threads = two semaphores; foo's starts with one permit.
  • A lock + Condition with a boolean turn is the general alternative.
  • With exactly two threads notify() is enough; with more use notifyAll().
  • Extending to three words: three semaphores or an int turn modulo 3.

leetcode-zeroevenodd.tldr:
• zero acts as a router: print 0, then hand the baton to odd or even based on the next number.
  • Each thread knows exactly how many turns it gets, so none waits for a turn that never comes.
  • The state-machine version needs notifyAll() because three threads share one monitor.
  • Test across many n and run orders.
leetcode-zeroevenodd.body:
Problem (paraphrased): a ZeroEvenOdd(n) instance is shared by three threads calling zero(), even() and odd(). Together they must print 0 1 0 2 0 3 … 0 n (as 010203…0n) using the provided printNumber.accept(x). zero prints only zeros, even only even numbers, odd only odd numbers.

Key idea: zero acts as a router: it prints 0 then hands the baton to odd or even depending on the next number; whoever prints hands the baton back to zero.

Solution 1 — three Semaphores

Java
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.function.IntConsumer;

class ZeroEvenOdd {
    private final int n;
    private final Semaphore zeroTurn = new Semaphore(1);
    private final Semaphore oddTurn = new Semaphore(0);
    private final Semaphore evenTurn = new Semaphore(0);

    public ZeroEvenOdd(int n) { this.n = n; }

    public void zero(IntConsumer printNumber) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            zeroTurn.acquire();
            printNumber.accept(0);
            (i % 2 == 1 ? oddTurn : evenTurn).release();   // route to whoever prints i
        }
    }

    public void even(IntConsumer printNumber) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i += 2) {
            evenTurn.acquire();
            printNumber.accept(i);
            zeroTurn.release();
        }
    }

    public void odd(IntConsumer printNumber) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i += 2) {
            oddTurn.acquire();
            printNumber.accept(i);
            zeroTurn.release();
        }
    }
}

Each thread knows exactly how many times it will run (n zeros, n/2 evens, (n+1)/2 odds), so nobody waits for a turn that never comes.

Solution 2 — one lock, a state machine and a shared counter

Java
import java.util.function.IntConsumer;

class ZeroEvenOdd {
    private final int n;
    private int next = 1;              // the next non-zero number to print
    private boolean zeroTurn = true;

    public ZeroEvenOdd(int n) { this.n = n; }

    public synchronized void zero(IntConsumer printNumber) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            while (!zeroTurn) wait();
            printNumber.accept(0);
            zeroTurn = false;
            notifyAll();
        }
    }

    public synchronized void even(IntConsumer printNumber) throws InterruptedException {
        printTurns(printNumber, false);
    }

    public synchronized void odd(IntConsumer printNumber) throws InterruptedException {
        printTurns(printNumber, true);
    }

    private void printTurns(IntConsumer printNumber, boolean wantOdd) throws InterruptedException {
        int count = wantOdd ? (n + 1) / 2 : n / 2;
        for (int k = 0; k < count; k++) {
            while (zeroTurn || (next % 2 == 1) != wantOdd) wait();   // my parity and not zero's turn
            printNumber.accept(next++);
            zeroTurn = true;
            notifyAll();                                            // three threads: must be notifyAll
        }
    }
}

Run it locally

Java
import java.util.stream.*;

public class ZeroEvenOddDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        for (int n = 1; n <= 12; n++) {
            for (int trial = 0; trial < 30; trial++) {
                ZeroEvenOdd z = new ZeroEvenOdd(n);
                StringBuffer out = new StringBuffer();
                Thread a = new Thread(() -> { try { z.zero(out::append); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } });
                Thread b = new Thread(() -> { try { z.even(out::append); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } });
                Thread c = new Thread(() -> { try { z.odd(out::append); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } });
                c.start(); b.start(); a.start();
                a.join(); b.join(); c.join();
                String expected = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n).mapToObj(i -> "0" + i).collect(Collectors.joining());
                if (!out.toString().equals(expected)) throw new AssertionError("n=" + n + " got " + out);
            }
        }
        System.out.println("1116 OK: n = 1..12, 30 runs each");
    }
}

leetcode-h2o.tldr:
• Semaphores cap a molecule at 2 H and 1 O; a CyclicBarrier(3) releases them together.
  • Atoms give back their permit only after releasing, so molecules can't mix.
  • A semaphore-only version (oxygen acquire(2)) serializes molecules: simpler, less parallel.
  • Validate every consecutive triple of output under random arrival orders.
leetcode-h2o.body:
Problem (paraphrased): hydrogen and oxygen threads arrive in any order and any number. Each must call its release function, but releases must happen in groups of three: exactly two hydrogens and one oxygen per molecule. A thread must wait until it can form a complete molecule; groups must not overlap.

Key idea: limit how many of each kind can be "in the current molecule" (semaphores with 2 H permits and 1 O permit), and make the three members wait for each other before anyone releases (a barrier of 3).

The semaphores decide who may join the molecule being built; the barrier decides when they may leave: only after all three have arrived. Because permits are returned only after releasing, the next molecule can't form until the current one is complete.

Solution 1 — Semaphores + CyclicBarrier (the textbook answer)

Java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

class H2O {
    private final Semaphore hSlots = new Semaphore(2);        // at most 2 H in the forming molecule
    private final Semaphore oSlots = new Semaphore(1);        // at most 1 O
    private final CyclicBarrier molecule = new CyclicBarrier(3);

    public H2O() { }

    public void hydrogen(Runnable releaseHydrogen) throws InterruptedException {
        hSlots.acquire();
        try {
            molecule.await();                                 // wait for the other two atoms
            releaseHydrogen.run();
        } catch (BrokenBarrierException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        } finally {
            hSlots.release();                                 // free my slot for the next molecule
        }
    }

    public void oxygen(Runnable releaseOxygen) throws InterruptedException {
        oSlots.acquire();
        try {
            molecule.await();
            releaseOxygen.run();
        } catch (BrokenBarrierException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        } finally {
            oSlots.release();
        }
    }
}

Why groups can't mix: the next molecule needs two H permits, and a hydrogen from the current group only returns its permit after printing. So no new group can complete the barrier until everyone in the current group has printed.

Solution 2 — Semaphores only (molecules serialized)

Java
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

class H2O {
    private final Semaphore hydrogenSlots = new Semaphore(2);
    private final Semaphore hydrogensReady = new Semaphore(0);

    public H2O() { }

    public void hydrogen(Runnable releaseHydrogen) throws InterruptedException {
        hydrogenSlots.acquire();          // only 2 hydrogens per molecule
        releaseHydrogen.run();
        hydrogensReady.release();         // tell oxygen one H is in
    }

    public void oxygen(Runnable releaseOxygen) throws InterruptedException {
        hydrogensReady.acquire(2);        // wait for both hydrogens of this molecule
        releaseOxygen.run();
        hydrogenSlots.release(2);         // molecule complete: open the next one
    }
}

Output is always HHO HHO … (hydrogens first in each triple), which satisfies the grouping rule. Simpler, but molecules form one at a time. acquire(2) takes both permits atomically, so two waiting oxygen threads can never each grab one hydrogen and stall.

Common wrong answers

  • Barrier only, no semaphores: three hydrogens can meet at the barrier and leave together (HHH).
  • Semaphores only, released before printing: atoms of the next molecule can print interleaved with the current one.
  • Counting with a shared int and notifyAll: workable, but easy to get group boundaries wrong; you must reset counters exactly when a group completes.

Run it locally — random arrival order, verifies every consecutive triple:

Java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class H2ODemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        for (int trial = 0; trial < 100; trial++) {
            int molecules = 1 + trial % 6;
            List<Character> atoms = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 0; i < molecules; i++) { atoms.add('H'); atoms.add('H'); atoms.add('O'); }
            Collections.shuffle(atoms);
            H2O h2o = new H2O();
            StringBuffer out = new StringBuffer();
            List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>();
            for (char a : atoms) threads.add(new Thread(() -> {
                try {
                    if (a == 'H') h2o.hydrogen(() -> out.append('H'));
                    else h2o.oxygen(() -> out.append('O'));
                } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { }
            }));
            threads.forEach(Thread::start);
            for (Thread t : threads) t.join();
            String s = out.toString();
            for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i += 3) {
                String g = s.substring(i, i + 3);
                if (g.chars().filter(c -> c == 'H').count() != 2) throw new AssertionError("bad group " + g + " in " + s);
            }
        }
        System.out.println("1117 OK: 100 random arrival orders, every triple is 2H + 1O");
    }
}

leetcode-fizzbuzz.tldr:
• Four threads share one counter; each owns the numbers matching its predicate.
  • wait/notifyAll with a predicate per thread is the most general solution.
  • A CyclicBarrier(4) per number keeps all threads in lock-step.
  • A semaphore dispatcher (number() routes) works if helpers precompute their turn counts.
leetcode-fizzbuzz.body:
Problem (paraphrased): a FizzBuzz(n) instance is shared by four threads: fizz() prints "fizz" for numbers divisible by 3 only, buzz() prints "buzz" for those divisible by 5 only, fizzbuzz() prints "fizzbuzz" for multiples of 15, and number() prints every other number. Together they must produce the FizzBuzz sequence from 1 to n in order.

Key idea: one shared counter i. For each i, exactly one of the four threads owns it; the others must wait until the counter moves past. Every thread loops until i > n.

Every value of i has exactly one owner, so at most one thread can make progress at a time; the other three wait. When i passes n, the last notifyAll() wakes everyone so they can see the loop is over and exit.

Solution 1 — synchronized + wait/notifyAll with a predicate per thread (most general)

Java
import java.util.function.IntConsumer;
import java.util.function.IntPredicate;

class FizzBuzz {
    private final int n;
    private int i = 1;

    public FizzBuzz(int n) { this.n = n; }

    private synchronized void serve(IntPredicate mine, IntConsumer action) throws InterruptedException {
        while (i <= n) {
            if (mine.test(i)) {
                action.accept(i);
                i++;
                notifyAll();               // wake everyone: the next owner could be any thread
            } else {
                wait();
            }
        }
    }

    public void fizz(Runnable printFizz) throws InterruptedException {
        serve(x -> x % 3 == 0 && x % 5 != 0, x -> printFizz.run());
    }
    public void buzz(Runnable printBuzz) throws InterruptedException {
        serve(x -> x % 5 == 0 && x % 3 != 0, x -> printBuzz.run());
    }
    public void fizzbuzz(Runnable printFizzBuzz) throws InterruptedException {
        serve(x -> x % 15 == 0, x -> printFizzBuzz.run());
    }
    public void number(IntConsumer printNumber) throws InterruptedException {
        serve(x -> x % 3 != 0 && x % 5 != 0, printNumber);
    }
}

When i passes n, the final notifyAll() wakes every waiter, they re-check i <= n, and all four exit.

Solution 2 — CyclicBarrier: all four threads walk 1..n in lock-step

Java
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.function.IntConsumer;

class FizzBuzz {
    private final int n;
    private final CyclicBarrier round = new CyclicBarrier(4);

    public FizzBuzz(int n) { this.n = n; }

    private void walk(java.util.function.IntPredicate mine, IntConsumer action) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            if (mine.test(i)) action.accept(i);        // exactly one thread matches each i
            try { round.await(); }                     // nobody moves to i+1 until i is printed
            catch (BrokenBarrierException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); }
        }
    }

    public void fizz(Runnable printFizz) throws InterruptedException { walk(x -> x % 3 == 0 && x % 5 != 0, x -> printFizz.run()); }
    public void buzz(Runnable printBuzz) throws InterruptedException { walk(x -> x % 5 == 0 && x % 3 != 0, x -> printBuzz.run()); }
    public void fizzbuzz(Runnable printFizzBuzz) throws InterruptedException { walk(x -> x % 15 == 0, x -> printFizzBuzz.run()); }
    public void number(IntConsumer printNumber) throws InterruptedException { walk(x -> x % 3 != 0 && x % 5 != 0, printNumber); }
}

Elegant, but it costs a barrier trip per number (four threads synchronize n times).

Solution 3 — Semaphores with number() as the dispatcher

Java
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.function.IntConsumer;

class FizzBuzz {
    private final int n;
    private final Semaphore fizz = new Semaphore(0), buzz = new Semaphore(0),
                            fizzbuzz = new Semaphore(0), num = new Semaphore(1);

    public FizzBuzz(int n) { this.n = n; }

    public void number(IntConsumer printNumber) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            num.acquire();                                 // wait until the previous i is printed
            if (i % 15 == 0) fizzbuzz.release();
            else if (i % 3 == 0) fizz.release();
            else if (i % 5 == 0) buzz.release();
            else { printNumber.accept(i); num.release(); }
        }
    }
    public void fizz(Runnable printFizz) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 3; i <= n; i += 3) {
            if (i % 5 == 0) continue;                      // multiples of 15 belong to fizzbuzz
            fizz.acquire(); printFizz.run(); num.release();
        }
    }
    public void buzz(Runnable printBuzz) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 5; i <= n; i += 5) {
            if (i % 3 == 0) continue;
            buzz.acquire(); printBuzz.run(); num.release();
        }
    }
    public void fizzbuzz(Runnable printFizzBuzz) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 15; i <= n; i += 15) {
            fizzbuzz.acquire(); printFizzBuzz.run(); num.release();
        }
    }
}

Each helper thread pre-computes how many turns it gets, so none waits for a turn that never comes — the same counting trick as 1116.

Common wrong answers

  • notify() instead of notifyAll(): it may wake a thread that doesn't own the next number; that thread waits again and the owner is never woken.
  • No exit check after waking: threads waiting when i passes n sleep forever and the program never terminates.
  • Each thread looping 1..n with its own counter and no coordination: output order is random.

Run it locally

Java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class FizzBuzzDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        for (int n = 1; n <= 31; n++) {
            for (int trial = 0; trial < 10; trial++) {
                FizzBuzz fb = new FizzBuzz(n);
                List<String> out = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
                List<Thread> ts = List.of(
                    new Thread(() -> { try { fb.fizz(() -> out.add("fizz")); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } }),
                    new Thread(() -> { try { fb.buzz(() -> out.add("buzz")); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } }),
                    new Thread(() -> { try { fb.fizzbuzz(() -> out.add("fizzbuzz")); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } }),
                    new Thread(() -> { try { fb.number(x -> out.add(String.valueOf(x))); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } }));
                ts.forEach(Thread::start);
                for (Thread t : ts) t.join();
                List<String> expected = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n).mapToObj(i ->
                    i % 15 == 0 ? "fizzbuzz" : i % 3 == 0 ? "fizz" : i % 5 == 0 ? "buzz" : String.valueOf(i)).toList();
                if (!out.equals(expected)) throw new AssertionError("n=" + n + " got " + out);
            }
        }
        System.out.println("1195 OK: n = 1..31, 10 runs each");
    }
}

leetcode-philosophers.tldr:
• Naive left-then-right fork picking deadlocks through circular wait.
  • Fixes: global lock ordering, a Semaphore(4) limiting diners, or tryLock on both forks with random back-off.
  • A single global lock is correct but lets only one philosopher eat at a time.
  • Test with CAS-based fork ownership checks and a timeout to catch deadlocks.
leetcode-philosophers.body:
Problem (paraphrased): five philosophers sit at a round table with one fork between each pair. To eat, a philosopher needs both adjacent forks. Implement wantsToEat(philosopher, pickLeftFork, pickRightFork, eat, putLeftFork, putRightFork) so that each call results in the philosopher eating, no two neighbours hold the same fork, and the system never deadlocks or starves. The method is called concurrently many times.

Why the naive version deadlocks: if every philosopher picks up their left fork at the same moment, each waits forever for the right fork held by a neighbour — a circular wait. Every correct solution breaks one of the deadlock conditions.

Convention used below: philosopher p has left fork p and right fork (p + 1) % 5.

Each philosopher sits between two forks, and the table is a ring. If every philosopher holds their left fork and waits for their right one, the waits form a cycle: a deadlock.

Solution 1 — global lock ordering (break circular wait): always lock the lower-numbered fork first. Philosopher 4 then picks fork 0 before fork 4, so the cycle can't close.

Java
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

class DiningPhilosophers {
    private final ReentrantLock[] forks = new ReentrantLock[5];

    public DiningPhilosophers() {
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) forks[i] = new ReentrantLock();
    }

    public void wantsToEat(int philosopher, Runnable pickLeftFork, Runnable pickRightFork,
                           Runnable eat, Runnable putLeftFork, Runnable putRightFork) throws InterruptedException {
        int left = philosopher, right = (philosopher + 1) % 5;
        ReentrantLock first = forks[Math.min(left, right)], second = forks[Math.max(left, right)];
        first.lock();
        second.lock();
        try {
            pickLeftFork.run();
            pickRightFork.run();
            eat.run();
            putLeftFork.run();
            putRightFork.run();
        } finally {
            second.unlock();
            first.unlock();
        }
    }
}

Solution 2 — let at most four sit down (break hold-and-wait for the whole table): with only four philosophers competing for five forks, at least one of them can always get both forks (pigeonhole), so progress is guaranteed.

Java
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

class DiningPhilosophers {
    private final ReentrantLock[] forks = new ReentrantLock[5];
    private final Semaphore seats = new Semaphore(4);

    public DiningPhilosophers() {
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) forks[i] = new ReentrantLock();
    }

    public void wantsToEat(int philosopher, Runnable pickLeftFork, Runnable pickRightFork,
                           Runnable eat, Runnable putLeftFork, Runnable putRightFork) throws InterruptedException {
        ReentrantLock left = forks[philosopher], right = forks[(philosopher + 1) % 5];
        seats.acquire();
        try {
            left.lock();
            right.lock();
            try {
                pickLeftFork.run(); pickRightFork.run();
                eat.run();
                putLeftFork.run(); putRightFork.run();
            } finally {
                right.unlock();
                left.unlock();
            }
        } finally {
            seats.release();
        }
    }
}

Solution 3 — try both forks or back off (break hold-and-wait per philosopher)

Java
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

class DiningPhilosophers {
    private final ReentrantLock[] forks = new ReentrantLock[5];

    public DiningPhilosophers() {
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) forks[i] = new ReentrantLock();
    }

    public void wantsToEat(int philosopher, Runnable pickLeftFork, Runnable pickRightFork,
                           Runnable eat, Runnable putLeftFork, Runnable putRightFork) throws InterruptedException {
        ReentrantLock left = forks[philosopher], right = forks[(philosopher + 1) % 5];
        while (true) {
            if (left.tryLock()) {
                try {
                    if (right.tryLock()) {
                        try {
                            pickLeftFork.run(); pickRightFork.run();
                            eat.run();
                            putLeftFork.run(); putRightFork.run();
                            return;
                        } finally { right.unlock(); }
                    }
                } finally { left.unlock(); }               // couldn't get the right fork: put the left back
            }
            Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1, 3));   // random back-off avoids livelock
        }
    }
}

Common wrong answers

  • Nested synchronized(left) { synchronized(right) { ... } } with no ordering: deadlocks under load (the grader often catches it as a timeout).
  • One global lock around everything: accepted, but only one philosopher eats at a time; interviewers will ask for better.
  • tryLock retry without back-off: can livelock as philosophers pick up and drop forks in lockstep.

Run it locally — the fork callbacks claim forks with CAS, so any overlap fails loudly:

Java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class DiningDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        DiningPhilosophers table = new DiningPhilosophers();
        AtomicIntegerArray forkOwner = new AtomicIntegerArray(new int[]{-1, -1, -1, -1, -1});
        AtomicInteger meals = new AtomicInteger();
        int mealsEach = 200;
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);
        List<Future<?>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int p = 0; p < 5; p++) {
            int ph = p, left = p, right = (p + 1) % 5;
            fs.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                for (int m = 0; m < mealsEach; m++) {
                    table.wantsToEat(ph,
                        () -> { if (!forkOwner.compareAndSet(left, -1, ph)) throw new IllegalStateException("fork " + left + " taken"); },
                        () -> { if (!forkOwner.compareAndSet(right, -1, ph)) throw new IllegalStateException("fork " + right + " taken"); },
                        meals::incrementAndGet,
                        () -> forkOwner.set(left, -1),
                        () -> forkOwner.set(right, -1));
                }
                return null;
            }));
        }
        for (Future<?> f : fs) f.get(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS);        // a deadlock would time out here
        pool.shutdown();
        System.out.println("1226 OK: " + meals.get() + " meals, no fork shared, no deadlock");
    }
}
Solution Breaks Concurrency Risk
Lock ordering circular wait good none if every path uses the order
Semaphore(4) hold-and-wait for the 5th good one extra primitive
tryLock + back-off hold-and-wait good livelock without randomized back-off
One global lock everything only one eats at a time correct but defeats the purpose

leetcode-boundedqueue.tldr:
• It's the producer–consumer buffer: one lock, notFull and notEmpty conditions, while loops.
  • Semaphores for free slots and filled slots plus a concurrent deque also work.
  • size() is only a snapshot under concurrency.
  • Test with several producers and consumers: nothing lost, nothing duplicated, bound respected.
leetcode-boundedqueue.body:
Problem (paraphrased): implement a thread-safe bounded FIFO queue with enqueue(element) (blocks while full), dequeue() (blocks while empty) and size(). Several producer and consumer threads use it concurrently. Don't use the JDK's BlockingQueue implementations.

Key idea: the producer–consumer buffer. One lock protects the deque; two conditions let producers and consumers wait for exactly the event they need.

Solution 1 — ReentrantLock + notFull / notEmpty

Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;

class BoundedBlockingQueue {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Deque<Integer> items = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();

    public BoundedBlockingQueue(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }

    public void enqueue(int element) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (items.size() == capacity) notFull.await();
            items.addLast(element);
            notEmpty.signal();                  // one item -> wake one consumer
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public int dequeue() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (items.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await();
            int v = items.pollFirst();
            notFull.signal();                   // one free slot -> wake one producer
            return v;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public int size() {
        lock.lock();
        try { return items.size(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

Solution 2 — Semaphores (slots and items) + a concurrent deque

Java
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedDeque;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

class BoundedBlockingQueue {
    private final ConcurrentLinkedDeque<Integer> items = new ConcurrentLinkedDeque<>();
    private final Semaphore freeSlots;
    private final Semaphore filledSlots = new Semaphore(0);

    public BoundedBlockingQueue(int capacity) { freeSlots = new Semaphore(capacity); }

    public void enqueue(int element) throws InterruptedException {
        freeSlots.acquire();
        items.addLast(element);
        filledSlots.release();
    }

    public int dequeue() throws InterruptedException {
        filledSlots.acquire();
        int v = items.pollFirst();          // a permit guarantees an element is present
        freeSlots.release();
        return v;
    }

    public int size() { return items.size(); }
}

Solution 3 — synchronized + wait/notifyAll

Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

class BoundedBlockingQueue {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Deque<Integer> items = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public BoundedBlockingQueue(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }

    public synchronized void enqueue(int element) throws InterruptedException {
        while (items.size() == capacity) wait();
        items.addLast(element);
        notifyAll();                 // producers and consumers share one wait-set
    }

    public synchronized int dequeue() throws InterruptedException {
        while (items.isEmpty()) wait();
        int v = items.pollFirst();
        notifyAll();
        return v;
    }

    public synchronized int size() { return items.size(); }
}

Common wrong answers

  • if instead of while before await(): with several consumers, two wake up for one item and the second dequeues from an empty deque.
  • One condition with signal(): may wake a producer when a consumer was needed; use two conditions, or signalAll/notifyAll with a single one.
  • A size field read outside the lock: stale values and torn invariants.

Run it locally — 4 producers, 4 consumers, checks nothing is lost or duplicated and the bound is respected:

Java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class BoundedQueueDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int capacity = 3, perProducer = 500, producers = 4, consumers = 4;
        BoundedBlockingQueue q = new BoundedBlockingQueue(capacity);
        Set<Integer> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        AtomicInteger maxSize = new AtomicInteger();
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(producers + consumers);
        List<Future<?>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int p = 0; p < producers; p++) {
            int base = p * perProducer;
            fs.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                for (int i = 0; i < perProducer; i++) { q.enqueue(base + i); maxSize.accumulateAndGet(q.size(), Math::max); }
                return null;
            }));
        }
        int total = producers * perProducer;
        for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) {
            fs.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                for (int i = 0; i < total / consumers; i++) {
                    if (!seen.add(q.dequeue())) throw new IllegalStateException("duplicate");
                }
                return null;
            }));
        }
        for (Future<?> f : fs) f.get(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        pool.shutdown();
        if (seen.size() != total || maxSize.get() > capacity) throw new AssertionError(seen.size() + " / max " + maxSize);
        System.out.println("1188 OK: " + total + " items, none lost or duplicated, max size " + maxSize.get());
    }
}

size() is only a snapshot under concurrency (another thread may change it right after it returns); that's expected and matches BlockingQueue.size() semantics.

leetcode-webcrawler.tldr:
• Hostname is url.split("/")[2]; claim each URL atomically with ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().add().
  • Level-by-level BFS on an executor is simple; a pending-task counter enables fully async crawling.
  • Increment the pending counter before submitting a child, so it can't reach zero early.
  • Follow-ups: per-host limits, politeness, distributed frontier with dedup.
leetcode-webcrawler.body:
Problem (paraphrased): given a start URL and an HtmlParser whose getUrls(url) returns the links on a page (a slow, blocking call), return every URL reachable from the start URL that has the same hostname, each exactly once, in any order. The single-threaded version is too slow; you must fetch pages concurrently.

Java
// Provided by LeetCode:
interface HtmlParser {
    java.util.List<String> getUrls(String url);
}

Key ideas: (1) hostname = url.split("/")[2] for http://host/path; (2) a concurrent set where add() returns false for already-seen URLs, which atomically claims each URL for exactly one thread; (3) know when the crawl is finished.

Solution 1 — level-by-level BFS with an executor (simple and robust)

Java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

class Solution {
    public List<String> crawl(String startUrl, HtmlParser htmlParser) {
        String host = hostOf(startUrl);
        Set<String> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        seen.add(startUrl);
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
        try {
            List<String> frontier = List.of(startUrl);
            while (!frontier.isEmpty()) {
                List<Future<List<String>>> pages = new ArrayList<>();
                for (String url : frontier) pages.add(pool.submit(() -> htmlParser.getUrls(url)));   // fetch the level in parallel
                List<String> next = new ArrayList<>();
                for (Future<List<String>> page : pages) {
                    for (String link : page.get()) {
                        if (hostOf(link).equals(host) && seen.add(link)) next.add(link);
                    }
                }
                frontier = next;
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            throw new RuntimeException(e.getCause());
        } finally {
            pool.shutdownNow();
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(seen);
    }

    private static String hostOf(String url) { return url.split("/")[2]; }
}

The main thread waits at the end of each level, which limits parallelism slightly when one page is slow.

Solution 2 — fully asynchronous with a pending-task counter (no level barrier)

Java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

class Solution {
    public List<String> crawl(String startUrl, HtmlParser htmlParser) {
        String host = startUrl.split("/")[2];
        Set<String> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        AtomicInteger pending = new AtomicInteger();
        CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(1);
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);

        class Visit implements Runnable {
            private final String url;
            Visit(String url) { this.url = url; }
            public void run() {
                try {
                    for (String link : htmlParser.getUrls(url)) {
                        if (link.split("/")[2].equals(host) && seen.add(link)) {
                            pending.incrementAndGet();                 // count BEFORE submitting
                            pool.execute(new Visit(link));
                        }
                    }
                } finally {
                    if (pending.decrementAndGet() == 0) done.countDown();   // last task out turns off the lights
                }
            }
        }

        seen.add(startUrl);
        pending.incrementAndGet();
        pool.execute(new Visit(startUrl));
        try {
            done.await();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        } finally {
            pool.shutdownNow();
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(seen);
    }
}

Correctness hinges on incrementing pending before submitting a child: the counter can then only reach zero when no task is running and none is queued.

Pitfall checking seen.contains(url) and then seen.add(url) is a check-then-act race; two threads can both crawl the same URL. add() alone is atomic and returns whether you won.

Common wrong answers

  • if (!seen.contains(u)) { seen.add(u); submit(u); }: two threads can both pass contains and crawl the same URL twice. Use the boolean returned by add.
  • Crawling with a parallel stream: getUrls blocks on I/O and the common pool has only cores − 1 threads.
  • Deciding completion with executor.awaitTermination: tasks keep submitting new tasks, so you must track pending work explicitly (latch, counter, or level-by-level BFS).

Run it locally — a fake parser with latency and a graph spanning two hosts:

Java
import java.util.*;

public class CrawlerDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, List<String>> web = Map.of(
            "http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/", List.of("http://news.yahoo.com/news", "http://news.google.com"),
            "http://news.yahoo.com/news", List.of("http://news.yahoo.com/us", "http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/"),
            "http://news.yahoo.com/us", List.of("http://news.yahoo.com", "http://news.google.com/us"),
            "http://news.yahoo.com", List.of("http://news.yahoo.com/news"),
            "http://news.google.com", List.of("http://news.yahoo.com/us"));
        HtmlParser parser = url -> {
            try { Thread.sleep(15); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
            return web.getOrDefault(url, List.of());
        };
        List<String> result = new Solution().crawl("http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/", parser);
        Set<String> expected = Set.of("http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/", "http://news.yahoo.com/news",
                                      "http://news.yahoo.com/us", "http://news.yahoo.com");
        if (!new HashSet<>(result).equals(expected) || result.size() != expected.size()) throw new AssertionError(result);
        System.out.println("1242 OK: " + new TreeSet<>(result));
    }
}

interface HtmlParser { List<String> getUrls(String url); }

Follow-ups interviewers ask: limit concurrency per host (a Semaphore per hostname); politeness delays and robots.txt; distributed crawling (partition URLs by hash of hostname across machines, a shared frontier in Kafka, dedup with a Bloom filter + persistent store); using virtual threads instead of a fixed pool since getUrls is blocking I/O.

leetcode-trafficlight.tldr:
• The intersection is a critical section and the light colour is shared state; one lock covers both.
  • Switch the light only when the arriving car's road isn't green.
  • A fair ReentrantLock prevents one road starving the other.
  • Verify that no two cars are ever inside and nobody crosses on red.
leetcode-trafficlight.body:
Problem (paraphrased): two roads (A = road 1, B = road 2) cross at an intersection with one traffic light; road A starts green. Cars arrive concurrently from both roads via carArrived(carId, roadId, direction, turnGreen, crossCar). A car may cross only when its road is green; if it isn't, the car must call turnGreen (switching the light to its road) before crossing. Cars from both roads must never be in the intersection at the same time, and the light must not be switched when it's already green for that road (no needless switches, no deadlock).

Key idea: the intersection is a critical section, and the light colour is shared state. One lock covers both "check the light, maybe switch it" and "cross", so the two can't interleave across roads.

Solution 1 — synchronized

Java
class TrafficLight {
    private int greenRoad = 1;                 // road A is green initially

    public TrafficLight() { }

    public synchronized void carArrived(int carId, int roadId, int direction,
                                        Runnable turnGreen, Runnable crossCar) {
        if (greenRoad != roadId) {             // only switch when needed
            turnGreen.run();
            greenRoad = roadId;
        }
        crossCar.run();
    }
}

Solution 2 — ReentrantLock (same logic, explicit lock, fair option)

Java
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

class TrafficLight {
    private final ReentrantLock intersection = new ReentrantLock(true);   // fair: cars served in arrival order
    private int greenRoad = 1;

    public TrafficLight() { }

    public void carArrived(int carId, int roadId, int direction, Runnable turnGreen, Runnable crossCar) {
        intersection.lock();
        try {
            if (greenRoad != roadId) {
                turnGreen.run();
                greenRoad = roadId;
            }
            crossCar.run();
        } finally {
            intersection.unlock();
        }
    }
}

The fair lock prevents a stream of cars on one road from starving the other road indefinitely; LeetCode accepts either.

Common wrong answers

  • Checking the light outside the lock and crossing inside it: two cars from different roads can both decide the light is theirs.
  • Calling turnGreen on every arrival: the problem counts unnecessary switches as wrong.
  • One lock per road: cars on different roads can then be inside at the same time.

Run it locally — checks that cars from both roads are never inside together and that switches only happen when needed:

Java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class TrafficLightDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        TrafficLight light = new TrafficLight();
        AtomicInteger inside = new AtomicInteger(), switches = new AtomicInteger(), crossings = new AtomicInteger();
        AtomicInteger currentGreen = new AtomicInteger(1);
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        List<Future<?>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int car = 1; car <= 400; car++) {
            int id = car, road = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextBoolean() ? 1 : 2;
            fs.add(pool.submit(() -> light.carArrived(id, road, road == 1 ? 1 : 3,
                () -> { if (currentGreen.getAndSet(road) == road) throw new IllegalStateException("needless switch"); switches.incrementAndGet(); },
                () -> {
                    if (currentGreen.get() != road) throw new IllegalStateException("crossed on red");
                    if (inside.incrementAndGet() != 1) throw new IllegalStateException("two cars inside");
                    crossings.incrementAndGet();
                    inside.decrementAndGet();
                })));
        }
        for (Future<?> f : fs) f.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        pool.shutdown();
        System.out.println("1279 OK: " + crossings.get() + " crossings, " + switches.get() + " light switches, never on red");
    }
}

qa.q: Why use a Semaphore instead of a lock for turn-taking problems (FooBar, ZeroEvenOdd)?
qa.a: Turn-taking means one thread unblocks another thread. A lock must be released by its owner, but a semaphore has no owner: thread A can release() thread B's semaphore. So "baton passing" maps directly onto semaphores, with one semaphore per turn and only the starting one holding a permit.

qa.q: In Print in Order, why is a CountDownLatch a good fit, and when isn't it?
qa.a: Each dependency ("second runs after first") is a one-time event, which is exactly what a latch models. It isn't suitable if the sequence must repeat (latches can't be reset) — then use semaphores or a stage counter with wait/notify.

qa.q: Why must FizzBuzz (4 threads) use notifyAll but FooBar (2 threads) can use notify?
qa.a: With two threads sharing a monitor, the only possible waiter is the other thread, so notify() wakes the right one. With four threads, notify() may wake a thread whose turn it isn't; it re-checks, waits again, and the thread that should run is never woken — a lost wakeup that stalls the program. notifyAll() (or separate Conditions per role) avoids it.

qa.q: How does the Building H2O solution prevent atoms of two molecules from mixing?
qa.a: Semaphores cap the forming molecule at 2 hydrogens and 1 oxygen, and a CyclicBarrier of 3 makes them release together. Atoms give back their semaphore permit only after releasing, so the next molecule can't gather its 2 H + 1 O (and trip the barrier) until every atom of the current one has finished.

qa.q: Name three ways to avoid deadlock in Dining Philosophers.
qa.a: Lock forks in a global order (lower id first) to break circular wait; allow at most four philosophers to compete via Semaphore(4); or use tryLock on both forks and release-and-retry with random back-off. A single global lock also works but serializes eating.

qa.q: In the multithreaded web crawler, how do you know the crawl is finished?
qa.a: Either process level by level and stop when a level yields no new URLs, or keep an atomic count of pending tasks: increment before submitting each child, decrement when a task finishes, and signal completion (a latch) when it hits zero. Incrementing before submission guarantees the count can't hit zero while work is still queued.

qa.q: Why is busy-waiting on a volatile flag a poor solution to these problems?
qa.a: It's correct for visibility but burns CPU continuously and starves the threads that need to make progress (especially with fewer cores than threads), which often causes LeetCode time-limit failures. Blocking primitives park the thread until it can proceed.

qa.q: How would you test your concurrency solution beyond LeetCode's grader?
qa.a: Run it thousands of times with threads started in random or all permutations, inject random small sleeps to widen race windows, assert invariants inside the callbacks (CAS-based ownership checks, counters for "inside the critical section"), always join with timeouts so deadlocks fail fast, and use tools like jcstress for memory-model level bugs.

cheat.leetcode-cheatsheet:
The problem set and the toolkit that solves all of it

  • Nine problems; three patterns solve almost all: semaphore baton passing, shared state + condition wait, barrier per round.
  • Semaphores fit turn-taking because a permit can be released by another thread.
  • Avoid busy waiting: it burns CPU and often times out.
  • Be ready to give a second solution with a different primitive.

1114. Print in Order

  • Two one-shot dependencies: CountDownLatch(1) per step is the most literal model.
  • Semaphores starting at 0 work too and can be reused if the sequence repeats.
  • A shared stage counter with wait/notifyAll generalizes to N steps.
  • Verify by starting threads in every permutation.

1115. Print FooBar Alternately

  • Strict alternation between two threads = two semaphores; foo's starts with one permit.
  • A lock + Condition with a boolean turn is the general alternative.
  • With exactly two threads notify() is enough; with more use notifyAll().
  • Extending to three words: three semaphores or an int turn modulo 3.

1116. Print Zero Even Odd

  • zero acts as a router: print 0, then hand the baton to odd or even based on the next number.
  • Each thread knows exactly how many turns it gets, so none waits for a turn that never comes.
  • The state-machine version needs notifyAll() because three threads share one monitor.
  • Test across many n and run orders.

1117. Building H2O

  • Semaphores cap a molecule at 2 H and 1 O; a CyclicBarrier(3) releases them together.
  • Atoms give back their permit only after releasing, so molecules can't mix.
  • A semaphore-only version (oxygen acquire(2)) serializes molecules: simpler, less parallel.
  • Validate every consecutive triple of output under random arrival orders.

1195. Fizz Buzz Multithreaded

  • Four threads share one counter; each owns the numbers matching its predicate.
  • wait/notifyAll with a predicate per thread is the most general solution.
  • A CyclicBarrier(4) per number keeps all threads in lock-step.
  • A semaphore dispatcher (number() routes) works if helpers precompute their turn counts.

1226. The Dining Philosophers

  • Naive left-then-right fork picking deadlocks through circular wait.
  • Fixes: global lock ordering, a Semaphore(4) limiting diners, or tryLock on both forks with random back-off.
  • A single global lock is correct but lets only one philosopher eat at a time.
  • Test with CAS-based fork ownership checks and a timeout to catch deadlocks.

1188. Design Bounded Blocking Queue (premium)

  • It's the producer–consumer buffer: one lock, notFull and notEmpty conditions, while loops.
  • Semaphores for free slots and filled slots plus a concurrent deque also work.
  • size() is only a snapshot under concurrency.
  • Test with several producers and consumers: nothing lost, nothing duplicated, bound respected.

1242. Web Crawler Multithreaded (premium)

  • Hostname is url.split("/")[2]; claim each URL atomically with ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().add().
  • Level-by-level BFS on an executor is simple; a pending-task counter enables fully async crawling.
  • Increment the pending counter before submitting a child, so it can't reach zero early.
  • Follow-ups: per-host limits, politeness, distributed frontier with dedup.

1279. Traffic Light Controlled Intersection (premium)

  • The intersection is a critical section and the light colour is shared state; one lock covers both.
  • Switch the light only when the arriving car's road isn't green.
  • A fair ReentrantLock prevents one road starving the other.
  • Verify that no two cars are ever inside and nobody crosses on red.
